$note: The protection the RELEASE TAGS are supposed to have, as a file. GitHub does not read this file —
nothing can, because a ruleset is settings rather than content. What it does is make the intent
reviewable, exactly as .github/branch-protection.json does for the branch.
Applied 2026-09-21 to ruleset id 23780086 via `POST /repos/{repo}/rulesets`. This is the body,
verbatim, so re-applying it is `gh api --method PUT repos/.../rulesets/23780086 --input` and
nothing translates it on the way.
Classic branch protection CANNOT do this: it does not govern tags. That is why Epic 5 step 3 of
FOUR PATTERNS, because four products share one tag namespace here — the same four release.yml
triggers on and the same four release-please cuts.
$decided: THE BYPASS LIST IS THE WHOLE DESIGN, and the operator chose on 2026-09-21: the GitHub App and
NOBODY ELSE. Not the operator, not a repository admin. A release tag can only be created by
`dew-flow-release-please`, which cuts it from a MERGED — therefore reviewed — release pull
request. That is what closes CWE-522 here rather than narrowing it.
The alternative considered and rejected was App-plus-operator, which leaves an emergency exit and
reduces the exposure to "an actor we trust" instead of removing it. It was rejected because the
exit is no longer needed: the release is held as a DRAFT until every target has an asset, so the
one repair that used to require touching a tag — a release published incomplete — cannot happen.
A bypass can be added in one line later; the reverse order never happens.
CREATION, UPDATE AND DELETION are all restricted. Creation alone would leave a protected tag that
can simply be MOVED to another commit, which is the same exposure with extra steps.
THE HONEST LIMIT, said rather than discovered: a ruleset restricts WHO may create a tag, not which
commit it points at. The commit becomes trustworthy because the only permitted creator cuts it
from a merged pull request — that chain, not the ruleset alone, is the guarantee.
VERIFIED, not assumed. Reading a ruleset back is not evidence it acts. A probe pattern
(`refs/tags/zz-ruleset-probe-*`) was added, a tag creation attempted with the operator's own
token, and refused — HTTP 422 `Reference update failed`. The pattern was then removed and no tag
name: release tags
